the sharding scales with DB size. e.g. TaskCache and Infra have no shards, TaskMeta has 4 shards and TaskData has 8 shards for vercel site.

It is true that this means we write out small fiels sometimes, but they don't survive for very long, they end up getting accumulated via 'intermediate' merge compactions

so yeah small commits will write more small files, but they don't accumulate over time.


  | canary | this PR
-- | -- | --
TaskData commit files under 1 MiB (31 builds) | 28 | 143
TaskMeta commit files under 1 MiB | 0 | 0

So correct, commits write more tiny files

but overall there are fewer SST files and meta files


  | canary | this PR
-- | -- | --
SST files in the final cache | 99 | 59
…of which under 1 MiB | 51 | 9
meta files in the final cache | 81 | 22

So the 'intermediate compaction' saves us in the near term and we generally end up with fewer files overall than the current policy.

Casandra and RocksDb solve this problem using novel approaches for small commits.  Rocks db uses a WriteAheadLog and a special L0 SST to accumulate small writes before sharding them.  Casandra is similar but simpler it just writes 'coarser' sharded SSTs when they are below a certain size.  I think we could do the casandra approach without too much difficulty.  This would be just another classificiation of 'top' files that don't respect sharding.  It isn't clear to me that we need it though/


The additional memory also scales with the family size, so yeah that is a concern.  Right now our TaskData writes will consume about 2x as much memory, we can address that by changing the sharding logic to delay splitting by shards until we hit a minimum size per shard (maybe 500K?)

pulls.title: Refactor fetchStrategy -> stage and completeness
pulls.body:
This is a refactor of the FetchStrategy type.

As the Partial Prefetching design has evolved, FetchStrategy has come to represent two independent concepts, which we now model separately: the _stage_ (AppStage) of the navigation that an entry was rendered through (shell, prefetch, or navigation), and the _completeness_ (Completeness) of the rendering through that stage (needs runtime request, cache complete but with dynamic holes, or fully complete with no dynamic holes). Everywhere that used to accept a FetchStrategy now accepts either one or both of these types.

(Note: I've called the type AppStage to distinguish it from the internal stages used on the server as part of the rendering algorithm. The stages used on the client are the ones we document publicly as part of `ensureStatic` and the `prefetch()` and `navigation()` APIs.)

The `completeness` field also replaces the `isPartial` field.

It's possible to express much of the logic using a single enum, as in the FetchStrategy model. To prove this, I've extracted most of the behavioral changes into earlier PRs, to make this one easier to review. But the resulting logic in the new model should be easier to follow. So on net, we have the same number of fields but expressed in a way that better fits the underlying design:

- Every prefetch task (e.g. a visible Link) has a target stage and level of completeness. The task finishes when the cache has entries that match _both_ targets.
- When deciding whether to overwrite an existing entry, a more less complete entry must never overwrite a less complete one, even if it represents a later rendering stage. For example, a response rendered at the Navigation stage cannot overwrite a response written at the Prefetch stage if it does not include cookie-dependent data; we must discard it and perform a new request.

pulls.title: Refactor the navigation fetch and decode layering
pulls.body:
Navigation and prefetch requests go through `createFetch`, which had grown several jobs beyond fetching. It decoded navigation responses itself (so React DevTools could time the request from the moment it was sent), with a flag for prefetches to opt out and a separate wrapper stream for HMR refreshes that can be superseded. With Cache Components, it also stripped the leading partial marker byte by rebuilding the Response around the stripped stream, and tee'd every response so a full prefetch could cut its shell from a second copy of the body. Every caller paid for the tee and the rebuilt Response, including ones that never needed them.

This PR untangles those layers. Each commit can be reviewed on its own.

This is mostly a restructuring, to make the subsequent PRs in the stack easier. No meaningful outward behavior changes.

pulls.title: turbo-tasks-backend: optimize aggregated updates outside of the lock
pulls.body:
### What?

Net the collectible counts of an `AggregatedDataUpdate` in a new `AggregatedDataUpdate::optimize()`, called after the follower task's lock has been released.

### Why?

When an aggregating task gains (or loses) an upper, `AggregatedDataUpdate::from_task` builds an update from the task's own collectible counts plus `+1` for every positive aggregated collectible.

- **Cancelling entries:** a task that takes or drops the collectibles of its subgraph holds an own `-1` for each of them, so most of those entries cancel out. An earlier large `next build` investigation found one such update with 106,268 entries, of which only 4 had a nonzero net count.
- **Serialization:** in a large `next build`, ~6,000 uppers connect the same task. `from_task` runs while that follower's lock is held, so anything done per update while the lock is held serializes across all workers.
- **Why the earlier version didn't help:** a previous version of this PR netted inside `from_task`, still under the lock. It didn't improve emit time.

### How?

- **`from_task`:** back to its original form (own entries, then `+1` per positive aggregated entry). It keeps a `Vec::with_capacity` upper bound so the vector isn't reallocated while the task is locked.
- **`optimize()`:** sums the collectible entries per collectible, drops zero sums, and keeps the dirty container update unchanged. It reuses the vector's allocation.
- **Call sites:** `optimize()` is called right after the follower lock is dropped, at the sites that apply the update to uppers afterwards. These are the new-follower paths and the lost-follower paths. In the lost-follower paths, `invert()` also moved out of the lock, after `optimize()`. The `balance_edge` paths, which hold both locks through `apply`, are unchanged.
- **Semantics:** applying the optimized update (or its inversion) gives the same final counts in the upper, and the same set of collectibles whose presence changes. Intermediate flips within one update can be skipped. Result order is unspecified.

**Tests:**
- Unit tests for summing, cancellation, mixed counts, empty and single entries, and disjoint keys.
- Equivalence of final counts and presence changes for add and invert.
- The real `optimize().invert()` path on `CollectibleRef`s, including the dirty container update.
- An integration test that reads an operation which takes its child's collectibles, through several root uppers.

**Measurement** on canary `8521c6ae0` (`bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages`, 32 CPUs, cold untraced builds, 1 warm-up plus 4 interleaved rounds, median of the paired per-round changes vs canary):

| | change |
|---|---:|
| `turbopack-emit` | **−32.2%** (17.4 s → 11.9 s) |
| "Compiled in" | −11.2% |
| wall | −10.0% |

All three were faster in all 4 rounds. Output (`.next` file set) and issues are unchanged vs canary. This is one VM and 4 rounds, and the gain isn't broken down between the preallocation and moving work out of the lock.

pulls.title: Emit the Turbopack shared-runtime bootstrap in the PPR resume so it gets the CSP nonce
pulls.body:
### What?

With `cacheComponents` and the default `experimental.turbopackSharedRuntime`, a Turbopack production build breaks hydration under a nonce-based CSP (`script-src 'self' 'nonce-…'`). The route's inlined chunk-group bootstrap ends up in the prerendered static shell without a nonce. The browser blocks it, the Turbopack runtime never starts the entry, and the page stays non-interactive.

This PR emits that bootstrap from the per-request part of the response instead, where the request's nonce is known. The shared runtime stays on by default.

### Why?

Since 16.4 the shared runtime replaces the per-route evaluate chunk with an inline `globalThis.TURBOPACK.push({ otherChunks, runtimeModuleIds })` script, passed to React as `bootstrapScriptContent`. A PPR static shell is rendered at build time: there is no request, so React has no nonce to put on it.

The shell can't be fixed when it's served either. On Vercel the proxy serves the cached shell before any Next.js code runs, and only the resumed dynamic stream is rendered per request. So the bootstrap has to come from that stream.

### How?

**Server.** Cache Components prerenders now keep the Turbopack bootstrap separate from the other bootstrap content, such as the Instant Navigation testing script, and leave it out of the shell.
- For a postponed shell, the resume emits it as an inline script with the request nonce, right before the inlined Flight data. This reuses the existing data-injection pipeline, so the ordering is the same as today: after the first HTML chunk for empty preludes, and for HTML- and data-postponed state on both the Node and web stream paths.
- A complete prerender emits it the same way, as part of the stored response.
- Fully dynamic renders and non-Cache-Components prerenders keep using React's `bootstrapScriptContent`.
- The paths that serve a postponed shell without a resume (the Instant Navigation testing lock and `__nextppronly` shell debugging) append the bootstrap themselves.

**Client.** A bootstrap pushed after the shared runtime has loaded is registered from inside that inline script. There, `document.currentScript` has no `src`, so `appBootstrap()` threw `Invalid URL` while deriving the asset prefix. That prefix is only used by the dev server's HMR WebSocket, so it's now only derived on the dev server. Dev behavior is unchanged.

**Not covered:**
- React's own `$RT` timing script in the static shell still has no nonce, so a nonce CSP still reports that one violation. It doesn't affect hydration, and it was already blocked before 16.4.
- Fully static pages under a nonce CSP are unchanged; their inline Flight data has no nonce either.

### Tests

New e2e suite `test/e2e/app-dir/ppr-shared-runtime-csp-nonce`. It runs on Turbopack production builds only (`@force-gate !dev && turbopack`) and covers:
- the shell contains no bootstrap, and the resume contains it exactly once with the request nonce
- the nonce is also picked up from a report-only CSP, and there is no nonce without a CSP
- the page hydrates under a nonce CSP
- the page hydrates when the bootstrap runs after the shared runtime and all entry chunks have loaded. The test forces that ordering deterministically, and it fails without the client change.
- fully static pages keep the inline bootstrap and hydrate

It fails on `canary` because the bootstrap is in the shell without a nonce and the page doesn't hydrate.

Existing suites run to check behavior didn't change:
- Turbopack start: `instant-navigation-testing-api` (this suite caught the late-bootstrap `Invalid URL` issue), `ppr-partial-hydration`, `partial-fallback-root-blocking`, `partial-fallback-shell-upgrade`, `csp-nonce-segment-scripts`, `next-dynamic-csp-nonce`, `static-shell-debugging`
- Webpack start: `csp-nonce-segment-scripts`
- Dev (Turbopack): `csp-nonce-segment-scripts`

I also checked by hand with the issue's reproduction (nonce CSP from `proxy.ts`): the page hydrates and only the `$RT` violation remains.

Not run: Vercel deploy and edge-runtime tests.

Fixes #99800

pulls.title: Keep requests through middleware in a single OpenTelemetry trace
pulls.body:
### What?

Requests that pass through middleware / `proxy.ts` now produce **one OpenTelemetry trace**, instead of two or three.

Before, with OTEL configured in `instrumentation.ts`:

| Request | No outer span | With an outer span (APM, custom server) |
|---|---|---|
| Middleware continues to render (`next()` / rewrite) | 3 traces (2 before 16.3) | 2 traces (1 before 16.3) |
| Middleware redirect / direct response | 2 traces (1 before 16.3) | 2 traces (1 before 16.3) |

After: 1 trace in every case.

### Why?

Two independent causes:

1. **Long-standing (13.5 → canary), #91282.** When middleware lets a request continue, the router server runs `BaseServer.handleRequest` twice: a middleware-invoke pass, then a render pass. Each pass extracts its context from the incoming request headers. Without an incoming `traceparent`, each pass started its own root trace.
2. **16.3 regression from #95306.** In-process Node.js middleware ran under `ROOT_CONTEXT` to make `Middleware.execute` a sibling of `handleRequest`. That also detached it from any outer span, so the middleware span always started an extra trace.

Customers upgrading 16.2 → 16.3 see this as "doubled traces".

### How?

When middleware lets a request continue, the render is always **nested inside the middleware span**, in every host:

```
next start / next dev:
 handleRequest GET (bubble, root)
  └─ middleware GET
      └─ GET /page

separately-invoked middleware (Vercel, adapters, direct entrypoints), no parent:
 middleware GET (root)
  └─ GET /page

host span / incoming traceparent P:
 P
  └─ middleware GET            (next start: P → handleRequest GET → middleware GET)
      └─ GET /page
```

**Middleware → render.** The middleware adapter forwards the `Middleware.execute` span's own W3C context (`traceparent` / `tracestate`, via the configured propagator) as request-header overrides on `next()` and rewrite responses. Every host already applies these overrides to the downstream request, including the `next start` router server, so no new host protocol is needed.
- Override lists replace the whole downstream header set. So:
  - **No user overrides:** the adapter lists every request header the middleware received, plus the trace headers.
  - **User overrides present:** they are kept, and the trace headers are added.
  - **User-set trace headers:** a `traceparent` / `tracestate` the middleware explicitly set (different from the one it received) wins. A value copied unchanged from the request, as with `new Headers(request.headers)`, is replaced so the render still nests.
- Redirects and direct responses are untouched.

**Request → middleware (self-hosted).** Once the middleware-invoke pass's `handleRequest` span is active, its W3C context is written onto the request headers. The middleware adapter (Node.js and the Edge sandbox) extracts it, so the middleware span is a child of that pass. The middleware-pass span keeps its existing name (`GET`); the route stays on the render-pass span. If there is no middleware span to forward (for example OTEL is registered only for Node.js while middleware runs on Edge), the render falls back to this context and still stays in one trace.

**#95306 regression.** The `ROOT_CONTEXT` detachment is removed, so an outer span, an incoming `traceparent`, or the middleware-pass span now parents Node.js middleware normally.

All of this only runs when OpenTelemetry is active and a valid span context exists. Without OTEL, no headers are added.

One-time initialization traces stay separate by design: instrumentation registration, route-module prewarming, and the once-per-process lazy `RouteModule.prepare` of direct entrypoints.

### Tests

- **New deploy-capable suite `test/e2e/app-dir/otel-middleware-single-trace`.** It runs Node.js `proxy.ts` and Edge `middleware.ts` with `@vercel/otel`. Middleware reports its active trace and span IDs; the render reports its active trace ID and the `traceparent` it received. The test asserts one trace and that the render's parent is the middleware span, so no collector is needed. It runs in dev, start and deploy mode, with no deploy gate. It covers:
  - continue to a page and to a route handler, plus rewrite, redirect and a direct response;
  - a request the middleware doesn't match, and an incoming `traceparent`;
  - user header overrides, including a deletion (the render still nests), and a user-set `traceparent`;
  - no internal `x-middleware-*` headers reaching the client.
- **Existing collector suite `test/e2e/opentelemetry/instrumentation`.** The middleware tests now assert **real** trace IDs and the exact shape: the render span's parent is the middleware span, the middleware span's parent is the middleware-pass `handleRequest` (self-hosted) or the external / host parent. They also check every span exported for the request.
  - **Setups:** default and direct-entrypoint hosting; Edge and Node.js middleware; root context and incoming `traceparent`.
  - **Requests:** page, route handler, rewrite and redirect.
  - **New variant:** direct entrypoints with a host parent span.
- **Unit tests** for the override helper (`forward-trace-context.test.ts`), including unchanged copied trace headers.

### Verification

- The new suite's nesting checks and the collector shape checks fail before this change (render parented to `handleRequest` or the external span) and pass after it.
- New suite passes in dev (Turbopack), start (Turbopack, webpack), and the same with `__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS=true`.
- Full `test/e2e/opentelemetry/instrumentation/` passes in start mode (Turbopack); the middleware tests also pass in dev (Turbopack) and start (webpack).
- Passed on the previous revision (not re-run for the nesting change): `test/e2e/opentelemetry/client-trace-metadata`, `test/e2e/app-dir/otel-parent-span-propagation`, `test/e2e/middleware-request-header-overrides`, and the W3C trace-header fetch-cache test in `test/e2e/app-dir/app-static`.
- Deploy: an earlier revision's trace-ID assertions passed on Vercel (default and Cache Components). The new parent-span assertion runs on Vercel for the first time in this revision's CI.

pulls.title: Write webpack dev manifests atomically
pulls.body:
### What?

In webpack dev, manifest files (`*manifest.json` / `*manifest.js`, e.g. `next-font-manifest.json` and `page_client-reference-manifest.js`) are now written atomically: the content goes to a temp file next to the manifest, which is then renamed over it. Other emitted assets are written as before.

### Why?

This fixes a canary hard flake in `test/e2e/app-dir/not-found/basic` › "should render the 404 page when the file is removed, and restore the page when re-added" ([example](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/38003705301/job/114068060547)). It is a real dev-server bug:

- Renaming `app/page.js` away makes `/` render `/_not-found`. That entry is already built, so the render doesn't wait for the in-flight rebuild.
- Webpack writes emitted assets in place (it truncates first). `RouteModule.loadManifests` can therefore read a 0-byte manifest. Instrumented local runs caught `.next/dev/server/app/_not-found/page_client-reference-manifest.js` (`Manifest file is empty`) and `.next/dev/server/next-font-manifest.json` (`Unexpected end of JSON input`). CI shows the same errors on every retry.
- The request returns a 500, the browser lands on the pages error page, which never recovers through app-dir HMR, and the test times out after 120 s.

Turbopack already writes its manifests with `writeFileAtomic` and isn't affected.

### How?

- `createAtomicManifestOutputFileSystem(fs)` returns an output FS that inherits from webpack's shared `graceful-fs` object without mutating it. Manifest writes go through the existing sync `writeFileAtomic` helper (`lib/fs/write-atomic.ts`, now accepting `Buffer`). That helper is the same one Turbopack's manifests use, and it already handles temp naming, cleanup and the Windows-tolerant `renameSync`. All other writes and methods go to the original FS.
- One wrapped FS is created next to the shared `inputFileSystem` and assigned to every compiler in the multi-compiler. The fallback compiler is wrapped too.
- This assumes the disk-backed dev output that Next.js uses. The dev server reads these manifests from disk with Node `fs` anyway.

### Verification

Full test file, `pnpm test-dev-webpack`, CI env (`NEXT_TEST_REACT_VERSION=18.3.1`, `__NEXT_EXPERIMENTAL_STRICT_ROUTE_TYPES=true`):

| | Runs | Manifest read errors | Failures |
|---|---|---|---|
| canary | 8 | 5 | 5 |
| this PR | 10 | 0 | 2* |

\* Both remaining failures happened at the *restore* step: an HMR refresh arrived before the app router initialized. That's a separate root cause, fixed independently in #100113, and with both PRs applied the file passed 10/10.

- `pnpm test-dev-turbo`: 3/3 passed. `pnpm test-start-webpack`: passed.
- After the switch to `writeFileAtomic`, with #100113's fix applied: 5/5 full-file `pnpm test-dev-webpack` runs passed in the same CI env, with no manifest read errors.
- Unit tests run against a real temp dir. They cover Buffer bytes being preserved and the target keeping its complete old content at the rename boundary (then the complete new one). They also cover errors reaching the callback exactly once, no leftover temp files, delegation of non-manifest writes, and the original FS not being mutated.

pulls.title: fix(analyze): use route summaries as the analyzer route index
pulls.body:
### What?

The bundle analyzer now uses the `route-summaries.json` that Turbopack writes as its **only** route index. This covers `next analyze`, `next build --analyze`, `next analyze export`, the analyzer UI's route picker, and comparison views. `routes.json` is no longer written or read, and `/_global-error` is listed like any other route.

### Why?

`next analyze export` failed with ENOENT on metadata routes that use `generateImageMetadata` or `generateSitemaps`, and the analyzer UI couldn't load their data either.

The cause was two route indexes that disagreed:

- Turbopack writes each route's `analyze.data` under its structural entrypoint key, e.g. `/icon` or `/sitemap.xml`. It also lists those keys in `route-summaries.json`, along with each route's sizes.
- `routes.json` was built separately from the routes manifest, which has the generator-adjusted pages `/icon/[__metadata_id__]` and `/sitemap/[__metadata_id__]`.

Readers turn each listed route straight into `<route>/analyze.data`, so they asked for files that were never written.

Since `route-summaries.json` already has every route plus its sizes, a second index is redundant. Dropping it makes the route list and the data on disk agree by construction.

### How?

- **Capture:** both capture commands read and validate the summaries, then use that list for the snapshot's `routeCount`. Nothing is filtered, so `/_global-error` (which can be large) is now visible.
- **Export:** `next analyze export` uses the same validated list, with the same `--route` filtering. If `route-summaries.json` is missing (some 16.4 canary snapshots predate it), the command fails with a clear message to re-run `next analyze`, without writing partial output.
- **UI:**
  - A shared helper derives each build's route list from its own summaries, for the current build, the baseline, and the route picker.
  - The comparison strip counts routes from the summaries rather than the `routeCount` saved in older snapshot metadata, which didn't include `/_global-error`.

**Compatibility:** older snapshots that have route summaries keep working. Snapshots captured while this bug was present export and compare correctly without re-capturing, because their summaries already use the structural names. Their stale `routes.json` is ignored.

### Tests

The `test/e2e/next-analyze` fixture now has a nested `generateImageMetadata` icon and a `generateSitemaps` sitemap. The suite checks, for both `next analyze` and `next build --analyze`, that:

- the summary route set, including `/_global-error`, has `analyze.data` for every route;
- exports emit exactly those routes;
- `routeCount` matches the summaries;
- `routes.json` is not written.

It also checks that a stale legacy `routes.json` is ignored, and that a snapshot without summaries fails with the re-capture message. I also exported a snapshot captured by the buggy published canary with the locally built CLI: it now exports `/icon` without re-capturing.

Fixes #99970

pulls.title: docs(cache-handlers): explain updateTags durations, fix Redis EX for Infinity
pulls.body:
Two small gaps left on the `cacheHandlers` page after #98039 rewrote it.

**`updateTags()` doesn't say what `durations` means.** The table calls it "optional expiration duration in seconds", but its presence is the signal: without it the call is an immediate invalidation (`updateTag()`, single-argument `revalidateTag()`); with it the tags go stale and entries carrying them may keep serving until `durations.expire` (`revalidateTag(tag, 'max')`). `revalidation-utils.ts` only passes `durations` when a profile resolves, so a handler that treats both cases the same loses stale-while-revalidate for profile-based revalidation.

**The Redis example passes `entry.expire` straight to `EX`.** `EX` needs a positive integer and `expire` can be `Infinity` ("never expire"), so that call fails for such entries. The example now omits `EX` when `expire` isn't finite and rounds up otherwise.

One file, docs only.

---

History: this PR originally corrected the `get()` guidance that told handlers to drop entries past `revalidate`. #98039 fixed that as part of the page rewrite, so this PR was rebased and reduced to the two items above.

pulls.title: fix(next-code-frame): snap visible window to char boundaries
pulls.body:
### What?

Fix a panic in `next-code-frame` when rendering error overlays for source code containing multi-byte characters (e.g. CJK).

### Why?

`extract_highlights()` used display-column values as byte offsets when computing the per-line scan window. For multi-byte characters (e.g. CJK: 3 bytes / 2 display columns), the window end could land inside a multi-byte character. `scan_template()`'s fallback then emitted spans with non–char-boundary offsets, causing `apply_line_highlights()` to panic when slicing the visible content string.

The crash depends on terminal width — different widths shift where the scan window lands, so the same source may or may not trigger it.

### How?

Snap the computed byte range to character boundaries using `floor_char_boundary` / `ceil_char_boundary` in `extract_highlights()`. Since the visible window is only an optimisation hint for the scanner, widening it slightly has no correctness impact.

Fixes #92641

pulls.title: fix(next/image): annotate Image export so deprecated props show as deprecated
pulls.body:
### Problem

The `@deprecated` tags on `next/image` props don't show up in the editor. If you write `<Image priority />` you get no strikethrough and no hint that you should use `preload` now.

The tags are there in `ImageProps`, they just never reach the user.

### Cause

`Image` is declared like this, with the return type inferred:

```ts
export const Image = forwardRef<HTMLImageElement | null, ImageProps>(...)
```

`ImageProps` lives in another file (`shared/lib/get-img-props`). When TypeScript expands a type alias from a different module during declaration emit, it drops the JSDoc of all the members. If the alias is in the same file the comments survive, cross file they don't.

This is what we ship today:

```ts
export declare const Image: React.ForwardRefExoticComponent<Omit<React.DetailedHTMLProps<...>, "src" | "height" | ...> & {
    preload?: boolean;
    priority?: boolean;   // the @deprecated is gone
    ...
} & React.RefAttributes<HTMLImageElement | null>>;
```

And this is what we get with the fix:

```ts
import type { ImageProps } from '../shared/lib/get-img-props';
export declare const Image: React.ForwardRefExoticComponent<ImageProps & React.RefAttributes<HTMLImageElement | null>>;
```

It recovers the tags for `priority`, `onLoadingComplete`, `layout`, `objectFit`, `objectPosition`, `lazyBoundary` and `lazyRoot`. So every deprecation added to the component since #83351 has been invisible.

### Is this breaking?

No. The old expanded type and the new one are assignable in both directions, and the props you get in autocomplete are the same (304 entries, same list). Only the way the type is printed changes. Now the deprecated ones are also marked as deprecated in the completion list.

The component is split in two (`ImageImpl` + the annotated export) only to keep the diff small. If I annotate the export directly, Prettier reformats the whole function body and the diff becomes 135 lines for a one line change.

### Test

`test/unit/image-component-deprecated-props.test.ts` compiles a small file that imports `next/image`, and checks that `getJsDocTags()` returns `deprecated` for each of those props. With the old declaration it fails 7 of 8 (the 8th one only checks the props resolve, and passes either way, so it works as a control).

I didn't use `expectTypeOf` like `infer-get-server-side-props-type.test.ts` does, because both types are assignable to each other, so a type equality check passes before and after the fix. It can't catch this.

### Alternative I tried

Turning `ImageProps` into an `interface` also fixes it, and it needs no changes in the component, because interfaces are always referenced by name in the emitted types. I didn't go that way because interfaces don't get an implicit index signature, so `const x: Record<string, unknown> = imageProps` stops compiling. `ImageProps` is public, so that would break users. Happy to switch if you prefer it.

Also worth noting: with `--isolatedDeclarations` TypeScript already rejects the current code with `TS9010: Variable must have an explicit type annotation`. So this annotation is what TS wants anyway.

pulls.title: turbo-tasks: lock-free priority queue for lowest-priority tasks, skip heap lock when empty
pulls.body:
### What?

Removes the global mutex from the turbo-tasks `PriorityRunner` ready queue for the hot paths, and makes `Queue::pop()` skip the remaining heap mutex entirely when the heap is empty.

Supersedes #94841: this is that PR rebased onto canary (keeping the keyed claim / inline execution from #96808), plus the empty-heap fast path, plus two simplification passes and review fixes.

### Why?

In a from-scratch build, nearly every scheduled task has the lowest priority (`TaskPriority::Initial`). Before this change, every `schedule` and every worker `pop` went through one `Mutex<Queue>`, which becomes a contention point at high worker counts.

### How?

**Queue split by band**
- `Executor<C, T, P>` declares `const LOWEST_PRIORITY: P` (`TaskPriority::Initial` for turbo-tasks). Items with that priority go to a lock-free MPMC `ConcurrentQueue` (FIFO; all items share a priority).
- All other priorities go to a `Mutex<BinaryHeap>` ordered by `P: Ord`. `pop` drains the heap first, then the lowest band.
- The heap starts with capacity 128 and only shrinks back to 128 when it becomes empty.
- Lock ordering: `pop` may take a `claimable` shard lock while holding the heap mutex; nothing takes the heap mutex while holding a shard lock.

**Scheduler / worker handshake**
- `schedule` takes no global lock. Liveness (no task stranded when the last worker retires) is a store-buffering pattern: the scheduler pushes then reads `active_workers`; a retiring worker decrements `active_workers` then re-checks the queue. Both sides put a `fence(SeqCst)` between their write and their read, so one of them always observes the other.
- The saturated hot path is push → `fence(SeqCst)` → `load`, so schedulers no longer write the shared `active_workers` cache line. Every worker that gives up its count goes through `decrease_active_workers` (`fetch_sub(AcqRel)` → `fence(SeqCst)` → re-check).

**One queued task per key**
- `Claimable::claim_key()` returns `Self::Key` (no `Option`): every task has a key.
- Queued tasks are stored by value in `claimable: FxDashMap<T::Key, (P, T)>`. The heap and the `ConcurrentQueue` only store `T::Key`.
- Pushing a key that is still queued **replaces** the queued task. The replaced task goes to the new `Executor::discard` hook (default: no-op). `TurboTasksExecutor::discard` balances the foreground job that `TurboTasks::schedule` began for it.
- This only applies to queued tasks: a task that `schedule` spawns directly never enters the queue.
- Claim = `claimable.remove(key)`. Pop = `claimable.remove_if(key, priority matches the band entry)`. Stale band entries are tombstones that a pop skips; a stale entry never takes a task queued again with a different priority. With the *same* priority it may take the newer task early, which only reorders equal-priority tasks.
- No per-task allocation or per-task mutex, no new `unsafe`. Keyed pushes/pops take a brief DashMap shard lock.

**Unique local-task keys**
- `ExecutionId` is a wrapping `u16`, so `ScheduleKey::LocalTask(ExecutionId, LocalTaskId)` was not unique across concurrent executions; with replacement that hung the build.
- The key is now `ScheduleKey::LocalTask(Option<TaskId>, ExecutionId, LocalTaskId)`. The remaining exception is two concurrent top-level executions (no parent task) sharing a wrapped `ExecutionId`.
- Local tasks stay in the runner (not plain tokio tasks) so readers can keep claiming them for inline execution.

**Empty-heap fast path**
- `heap_non_empty: AtomicBool` is written only under the heap lock. `pop()` checks it and goes straight to the lowest band when the heap is empty, so the common cold-build pop never touches the heap mutex.
- A stale `true` costs only an unnecessary lock. A stale `false` can't hide a push that must be observed, by the same fence handshake.

### Tests

- `priority_runner` tests use plain `u32` priorities. New: `heap_only_shrinks_when_empty`. The saturated-path regression test is now `stress_saturated_schedule_vs_retiring_worker`.
- Replacement within and across bands, claims in both bands, stale entries, concurrent same-key producers/poppers/claimer, claim-vs-pop exactly-once, band ordering, heap-flag drain/refill, pop not waiting on the empty heap's lock, three liveness stress tests.
- Stress tests use a timer-only tokio runtime: with `enable_all()` on `wasm32-wasip1-threads`, newly spawned tasks reproducibly stopped being polled.
- On canary `b24905530`: `turbo-tasks` 134 passed (two full runs), `turbo-tasks-backend` 282, wasi lib 110 passed, `priority_runner` 5× repeated, clippy `-D warnings`, fmt. Cold 32-core `next build` of `bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages` completes (one run, 34.3 s compiled / 59 s wall; not a benchmark).

### Benchmarks

`bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages`, cold `next build` (Turbopack), `taskset` CPUs = `TURBO_TASKS_AVAILABLE_PARALLELISM` workers.

Current head (`4d89cde5`) vs its base canary (`b24905530`), both fresh release builds of the native bindings with the same JS. Per CPU count: 1 warm-up per arm, then 4 interleaved untraced rounds per arm (medians):

| CPUs = workers | canary wall | this PR wall | Δ wall | canary "Compiled in" | this PR "Compiled in" | Δ compiled | paired per-round wall Δ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 8 | 93.5 s | 93.0 s | −0.5% | 52.5 s | 51.5 s | −1.9% | −3.3 … +8.1% |
| 16 | 73.6 s | 72.5 s | −1.4% | 42.5 s | 41.5 s | −2.4% | −5.9 … +4.4% |
| 32 | 69.5 s | 59.2 s | **−14.8%** | 45.5 s | 34.0 s | **−25.2%** | −25.4 … −5.3% (all 4 faster) |

`whole app module graph` span, from 2 light-traced runs per arm (`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=next_api=info`); busy cores are system-wide `/proc/stat` over the span, as a share of the pinned CPUs:

| CPUs | canary span | this PR span | Δ | busy cores, canary | busy cores, this PR |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 | 9.56, 9.16 s | 8.91, 8.81 s | −5% | 6.6 of 8 | 6.7 of 8 |
| 16 | 7.67, 6.99 s | 5.76, 5.69 s | −22% | ~11 of 16 | ~12 of 16 |
| 32 | 10.36, 12.35 s | 5.60, 5.94 s | **−49%** | ~12 of 32 | ~23 of 32 |

At 8 and 16 CPUs the wall-time differences are within run-to-run noise. At 32 CPUs, canary keeps only ~12 cores busy during the module graph; this PR roughly doubles that and halves the phase.

Earlier passes, for history: the first version of this PR measured 77.5 s → 57.9 s wall at 32 CPUs (older base). The first simplification pass showed no measurable difference to the version before it (8 rounds at 32 CPUs: 63.4 s → 62.2 s median wall, paired per-round median +0.3%).

Review-round microbenchmarks (scratch harnesses, not committed):
- `ConcurrentQueue` vs `crossbeam_queue::SegQueue`: SegQueue was 16–30% slower at 16/32 threads with split producers/consumers and 3–18% slower with mixed push/pop at 32 threads (two runs), so `ConcurrentQueue` stays and no full build benchmark was run.
- `fetch_add(0)` RMW vs fence + `load` on the saturated path: 1.97 s vs 1.94 s median for 4.8M schedules, within noise. No speedup is claimed.
- Layout: `PriorityRunner` is already 128-byte aligned (via `ConcurrentQueue`'s `CachePadded`), so extra padding isn't needed.

Caveats: single VM, one session, 4 untraced and 2 traced rounds per arm, no statistical test; the CPU counts ran one after another, so cross-CPU-count comparisons can include drift. The AtomicBool's own effect isn't isolated.

pulls.title: [turbopack] Fix two GC paths that leave half-torn-down dependency edges
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes two GC bugs that each lead to a reported Turbopack panic when GC and persistent caching are both on:

```
task TaskId N (invalidate cell dependents, MustExist): task is missing in memory or persistent storage — a stale reference to an already-collected or never-created task
```

**Interrupted GC pass + eviction.** When a GC pass is interrupted, tasks would be marked deleted but tombstones would not be written. Eviction still dropped every `deleted` task anyway. The next snapshot then persisted the neighbours' halves of the torn-down edges, while the collected tasks' last snapshot stayed live on disk. A later lookup restored such a task as live and clean, with children that GC had since collected and tombstoned. Touching those children panics with `MustExist`.

   - Solution: eviction should not drop `deleted` tasks if the snapshot was interrupted


**Resurrected task keeps stale reverse edges.** When GC collects a task `P`, it scrubbed the forward edge from each dependent `D` but deliberately left `P`'s own `cell_dependents` / `output_dependent`, since `P` was being deleted. If `P` was then resurrected, that stale entry survived. When `D` was collected later it had no forward edge to `P`, so the entry was never cleared, and the next time `P` updated the cell it panicked on the missing `D`. This only shows when `D` is inactive: a live `D` gets dirtied by `P`'s update, re-executes, and re-registers a fresh edge pair, which hides it.

   - Solution: GC should not assume 'deleted' tasks are always deleted! resurrection defeats it

pulls.title: Reland experimental custom webpack support
pulls.body:
### What?

Reland [#98862](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/98862) after its revert in [#99227](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/99227). Restore `next dev --custom-webpack` and `next build --custom-webpack`, CLI documentation, and the original e2e fixture, **without declaring webpack as a peer dependency**. `--webpack` continues using bundled webpack.

### Why?

Allow applications to explicitly opt into their installed webpack version. The CLI records the absolute application directory before loading dev/build internals; config loading validates webpack, while Next.js's compiled webpack wrapper uses a project-scoped `createRequire` for every webpack import. This ensures `next.config.js`, user plugins, and Next.js compilation use the same webpack even if a different version is visible from inside the `next` package. Custom mode installs no webpack aliases; bundled mode keeps its explicit alias list.

### How?

Restore the feature on post-revert canary without undoing intervening changes (including `next analyze`). Keep webpack as an application-installed dependency checked at opt-in time, rather than an npm peer in `next`'s published metadata. The e2e tests exercise webpack 5.98.0 and 5.111.0 in dev and production, config-time `require('webpack/package.json')`, custom and built-in plugins, the missing-install diagnostic, bundled fallback, and conflicting flags. A regression fixture disables pnpm hoisting and shadows webpack 5.98.0 beside `next` while the app installs 5.111.0; it proves Next still selects the app's instance. Another test builds with an explicit application directory from a different cwd. A dedicated Custom Webpack guide (shared between App and Pages Routers) includes install/usage examples and a pnpm `hoistPattern` note for plugins and workspace tooling that independently resolve webpack; both CLI option rows link to the guide.

**Internal-sync caveat:** #99227 reports that declaring webpack as an optional peer introduced a dependency chain that duplicated Next.js in monorepos and broke internal sync. This reland **omits the peer declaration** to avoid that specific graph edge, while keeping runtime validation for `--custom-webpack`. The private dependency graph and sync reproduction are unavailable here; local tests do **not** independently prove internal sync is fixed. Maintainers should verify it before merging.

**Local verification:** focused e2e **8/8 dev and 8/8 production** (plus targeted non-isolated checks for the two new tests), Next.js build and types, frozen lockfile install, changed-file ESLint, Prettier, and `pnpm types-and-precompiled` from a clean commit (no generated diff). Repo-wide `pnpm lint-eslint .` fails with a plugin-scope configuration error on the post-revert base as well (`import/no-extraneous-dependencies` cannot find plugin `import`); changed-file lint passes.

**Review follow-up:** Restored the bundled-only `webpack/package` metadata alias and added config-time coverage for both extensionless and `.json` metadata imports. Per sokra's direction, no runtime version validation is added; the docs explicitly describe custom webpack as use at your own risk and list the tested versions without guaranteeing compatibility.

**CI note:** Commit `51ebc4f9` passed docs-link, lint, types/precompiled, all production tests and changed-test flake runs, but a new explicit-directory case attempted `next build` inside a dev-mode shard and failed deterministically with a missing `.next/dev/trace`. The follow-up test-only commit `9d5c3d4e` instead exercises `next dev <appDir>` there and checks its HTTP output; it preserves the production `next build <appDir>` assertion. Focused dev and production e2e tests pass 8/8 locally; That commit's CI passed. Review follow-up `ed1c7bd0` also passed CI. The docs-only commit `10cbbd84` moves the setup section into the dedicated guide; its CI is running. The earlier docs-only commit also hit unrelated instant-validation snapshot mismatches, which were not rerun as flakes.

pulls.title: Optimize esm exports by shifting the protocol burden to getters
pulls.body:
To support live bindings and cyclic references we bind esm exports as getter properties.  However this is ambiguous with binding raw values, so we would always use `0` as a tag to flag that the next value was a _value_ not a getter function.

In practice value exports account for 90% of exports and getters only 10% (from vercel-site).  So this changes the protocol so the getter functions require tags instead saving a small number of bytes in the output.

pulls.title: Assert transient task references are not serialized
pulls.body:
### What?
Assert in debug builds that transient `TaskId`s and packed `RawVc` references are not serialized by bincode or serde.

### Why?
Transient tasks do not survive a restart. #99383 avoids serializing suspended operations by waiting for them to settle; this encoding-time guard catches transient references that reach any remaining serialization path.

If we don't filter transient task references, then warm builds attempt to recover missing tasks which is ambiguous with a GC bug.

### How?
Replace the derived bincode `Encode` and serde `Serialize` implementations for both types with equivalent implementations that validate transience before delegating to the same underlying fields. Existing wire formats, deserialization, and release-mode behavior remain unchanged.

Stacked on #99249, above #99383.

pulls.title: Show async module scope in bundle analyzer
pulls.body:
### What?

Show source load scope in the bundle analyzer's single-build view: label async-only and mixed sources in the table, mark them in the treemap with a legend, and add an **Initial only** filter.

### Why?

Help distinguish sources reachable only behind an async import boundary from sources reachable through an initial path (or both). This describes **module-graph reachability**, not when a browser actually requests a chunk.

### How?

Traverse the route's active-entry module graph, propagating initial, async, and traced reachability across dependencies. Combine the reached module scopes for each source, then pass the resulting classification to the table, treemap, and filter. The new filter and indicators apply to the single-build view; the comparison view keeps its existing behavior.

**Verification:** Bundle-analyzer typecheck, focused lint/format checks, and production build passed; all eight combinations of the scope flags were checked when simplifying the classification logic.

pulls.title: improve disk read semantics around MustExist and AllowMissing
pulls.body:
Ensure two concurrent reads of a missing task both observe it as missing: `AllowMissing` returns `None` for both, and `MustExist` panics for both, rather than letting one reader mistake an intermediate blank entry for a task. A missing requested Data or Meta key is conclusive; the restore path also avoids retrying that key in a busy loop.

Add focused coverage for `task_pair`, `prepare_tasks`, missing categories, and restore races. Stacked on #99383, which removes suspended-operation serialization; this PR no longer filters persisted operations.

## Summary

The rollback in #99285 keeps local-only modules unsplit by default to avoid the remote-components singleton regression in #99279. This follow-up preserves facade-backed export mangling as an **opt-in** for applications that benefit from shorter keys even when a namespace escapes.

pulls.title: Measure AI upgrade nudges, handoffs, and completion
pulls.body:
> [!TIP]
> Recommended to review commit by commit with "Hide whitespace" enabled.

### Why?

Measure how often humans and agents receive upgrade nudges, start AI upgrades, and finish them.

### How?

Record the configured policy, shown nudges, human decisions, AI upgrade runs, CLI results, and agent results through existing Next.js telemetry. Existing telemetry opt-out settings apply.

`next upgrade --ai` prepares an upgrade prompt and hands it to an agent. The prompt asks the agent to run `next internal report-ai-upgrade <run-id> success|failure` after completing the upgrade and verification. The run ID links this report to the original upgrade run.

Completion reporting depends on the agent following that instruction. A missing report means unknown, not failure. The prompt does not instruct the agent to hide reporting or require it to mention the telemetry submission to the user. The reporting command suppresses the normal telemetry notice.

Closes NAR-938

pulls.title: Remove suspend during operations
pulls.body:
## What

Remove the ability to suspend in flight operations to allow for snapshotting and GC

## Why

Exstensive testing with GC has revealed a number of bugs latent in this system

* transient task ids are getting serialized as part of operations, this confuses our new stricter task access semantics in fresh sessions
* child execution contexts don't properly participate, they both need to suspend when requested to avoid exceeding retries since the task they are waiting for has already suspended, and cannot suspend because that could deadlock the scope_bounded call

Instead we just don't suspend.  This simplifies a lot, should be a small perf win (purely from not touching the atomics as often)

The major risk is that waiting for everything to settle adds latency.  To mitigate that:

* idle snapshots don't wait for operations to settle, they just bail out instead
* other snapshots do wait but log warnings if it takes more than 10s, this should never happen but if it does we will have a smoking gun

pulls.title: Add unstable parameter matching APIs
pulls.body:
## Summary

Let Cache Components applications configure parameter matching separately from build-time prerenders. `generateStaticParams` continues to supply concrete examples; the new `unstable_paramMatching` and `unstable_generateParamMatching` exports control whether a novel value returns 404, blocks on generation, receives a fallback shell, or stays dynamic.

With `cacheComponents: true`:

```ts
// app/[lang]/layout.tsx
export const unstable_paramMatching = { lang: 'not-found' }

// app/[lang]/catalog/[top]/items/[bottom]/page.tsx
export const unstable_paramMatching = {
  top: 'blocking',
  bottom: 'fallback',
}

export function generateStaticParams() {
  return [{ lang: 'en', top: 't1', bottom: 'b1' }]
}
```

This prerenders `/en/catalog/t1/items/b1`. A language other than `en` returns 404. On a cache miss, `/en/catalog/t2/items/b2` blocks on generation, while `/en/catalog/t1/items/b2` can receive fallback UI immediately. `dynamic` keeps a parameter out of prerenders.

Alternatively, `export async function unstable_generateParamMatching()` returns the same partial object. It takes no arguments and runs independently of `generateStaticParams`, once per module within each route evaluation. Public `use cache` helpers are supported. No additional configuration flag is required, and `ParamMatching` from `next` provides optional strict typing.

Policies merge from layouts toward pages, with descendants overriding only supplied keys:

- A module can configure parameters at or above its segment. Explicit modes must follow URL order: `not-found → blocking → fallback → dynamic`.
- A `not-found` parameter requires every preceding parameter to be explicitly `not-found`, too. Every route or parallel branch sharing that parameter definition must agree.
- Unconfigured parameters retain inference. An unconfigured tail without examples stays dynamic; explicitly dynamic parameters cannot be included in prerenders.
- Shell validation follows explicit fallback boundaries instead of silently replacing them with blocking behavior; `instant = false` opts out of that validation. With these APIs, `output: 'export'` requires all parameters to be explicitly `not-found`.
- `unstable_ensureStatic = 'navigation'` allows `blocking` and `not-found`, but rejects effective `fallback` and `dynamic` policies in both builds and development. It still requires complete `generateStaticParams` examples and fully static server output, even with `instant = false`. Supporting fallbacks for fully static navigations is deferred to a follow-up.

Runtime admission, cache regeneration, and client route discovery preserve those boundaries. Adapter output uses the existing routing contract, including prefixed query keys for root fallbacks.

## Verification

- Unit and integration coverage for policy merging, validation, generated types, shell selection, blocking/fallback behavior, navigation, parameter encoding, revalidation, and root-cache isolation.
- Real fixtures cover direct, inherited, generated, and parallel-slot combinations with `ensureStatic`, including valid overrides, missing examples, dynamic-data errors, and preserved closed prefixes. Both bundlers and both Partial Prefetching settings are covered in build/start and dev.
- Existing `ensure-static-navigation` build/dev validation and `ensure-static-navigation-runtime` production suites pass without changing their fixtures or validation implementation.
- Routing, generator, and root-parameter fixtures have passed real adapter deployment tests in both ordinary and Cache Components jobs. Local adapter-output assertions separately check the root-fallback query contract.
- [ ] Confirm cold open-suffix requests and revalidation in a deployment known to use grouped functions, and verify rejected prefixes do not invoke a function or consult ISR. Passing HTTP assertions alone does not establish these properties.

pulls.title: Allow skipping React and ESLint upgrades
pulls.body:
Stacked on #99471.

### Why?

Upgrading React or ESLint can cause peer dependency conflicts. After restoring compatible versions, retrying the upgrade can bump them again.

### How?

Add `--skip-react-upgrade` and `--skip-eslint-upgrade` to skip the corresponding dependency updates and codemods. The React flag also preserves types and overrides.

Add troubleshooting checklists to the version guides and point upgrade agents to them. Required migrations still need to be completed before verification; if Next.js already matches the target, run the interrupted migrations individually.

pulls.title: Prefer the declared package manager during upgrades
pulls.body:
### Why?

Running a codemod through `npx` can select npm even when the app declares Yarn, pnpm, or Bun, causing dependency installation to fail.

### How?

Read `package.json#packageManager` before `npm_config_user_agent`. Keep the existing user-agent, lockfile, and npm fallbacks unchanged.

Add shared checks for installation and recovery after an interrupted upgrade.

pulls.title: Pass App Page HMR state through a dev render context
pulls.body:
## Summary

Continue decoupling App Router rendering from incoming request objects by capturing HMR state at the handler boundary and passing it through DevRenderContext.

The context contains the HMR refresh hash and shared server-component HMR cache, and is constructed only under `next dev`. Production omits this state, and prerendering does not consume it. Rendering no longer reads the hash from request metadata. Existing upstream metadata transport and cache invalidation behavior are preserved; status and debugging callbacks are left for separate migrations.

## Verification

- `pnpm test-dev-turbo test/development/app-dir/use-cache-dev/use-cache-dev.test.ts` (7 tests)
- `pnpm test-dev-webpack test/development/app-dir/use-cache-dev/use-cache-dev.test.ts` (7 tests)
- `pnpm test-start-webpack test/e2e/app-dir/app/standalone.test.ts` (isolated production build and Edge coverage)

pulls.title: turbo-persistence: intermediate merges take the newest files of similar size
pulls.body:
## Summary

Stacked on #99268.

An intermediate merge merged every file above a shard's bottom run. Small commits, such as the snapshots of a development session, write small files: they push a shard over `max_files_above_bottom` quickly, and the merge then rewrote the large files of earlier build-sized commits along with them.

Like the size ratio of RocksDB's universal compaction, an intermediate merge now takes the newest file, and then each next older one while it's at most `size_ratio_percent` (default 100%) larger than the files taken so far, with at least the two newest. Small files are merged with each other; a large file only joins once the newer files add up to about its size. Because the merge always takes the newest files, its output can still be placed after all existing files, and the older files it leaves out stay older.

The trigger (`max_files_above_bottom`) and bottom merges are unchanged.

## Verification

- A selector simulation where every build-like commit is followed by ten tiny commits: write amplification **6.43 → 1.98**, with the same maximum of 5 files per shard. The build-only simulation is unchanged (space amplification 1.34, write amplification 1.25).
- Selector tests: small files after a large one merge without it; similar sizes all merge; steeply growing sizes merge at least the two newest; the ratio boundary.
- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence`, `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --tests`, and the Miri job's command for turbo-persistence pass.
- End to end, 31 consecutive vercel-site builds with GC on (about half the TaskData commits are small), against #99268:

  | | #99268 | this PR |
  |---|---|---|
  | compaction bytes written per byte committed | 1.61× (12.52 GB) | **1.45×** (10.99 GB) |
  | …by intermediate merges | 3.69 GB | **2.34 GB (−37%)** |
  | …by bottom merges | 8.82 GB | 8.66 GB |
  | cache size, final / max | 2.94 / 3.24 GB | 2.92 / 3.13 GB |

  Intermediate merges run more often (126 vs 104 TaskData jobs) but each rewrites less. A development session, with many small snapshot commits, should benefit more.

<!-- NEXT_JS_LLM -->

pulls.title: turbo-persistence: space-amplification driven compaction with adaptive hash shards
pulls.body:
## Summary

Turbo-tasks GC can only shrink the persistent cache if compaction merges each tombstone with the data it deletes. Canary's compaction algorithm leaves many tombstones behind so with GC enabled the cache is only 5% smaller than without it. This PR replaces compaction with a space-amplification policy on hash shards, modeled on RocksDB universal compaction and Cassandra UCS. With GC enabled, the cache stays ~flat.

### Cache size over 31 consecutive vercel-site builds

Same canary base and the same commits in every arm. The size is measured after each build, including its compaction on shutdown.

| build | canary, GC off | canary, GC on | this PR, GC off | this PR, GC on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.59 GB | 2.60 GB | 2.63 GB | 2.64 GB |
| 10 | 3.15 GB | 3.12 GB | 3.24 GB | 3.07 GB |
| 20 | 3.42 GB | 2.92 GB | 3.20 GB | 3.06 GB |
| 22 | 4.57 GB | 3.87 GB | 3.55 GB | 3.18 GB |
| 31 | **4.19 GB** | **3.96 GB** | **3.75 GB** | **3.00 GB** |
| growth, build 1 → 31 | +1.60 GB | +1.36 GB | +1.12 GB | **+0.36 GB** |

- **GC saves 5% with canary's compaction and 20% with this one** (final size, GC on vs. off). A full compaction of the final cache puts the live data at about 2.8 GB, so this PR with GC is within about 8% of it.
- **Build 22 rewrites a lot of task data.** Canary grows by about 1 GB at that build in both modes and never recovers the space. This PR absorbs it and merges the superseded versions away within a few builds.

### Why canary's compaction can't keep up with GC

- **Old versions and tombstones don't reliably meet the data they supersede.** Canary wrote recently read keys and the rest into separate warm and cold files and never merged across them.
- **Its merge triggers couldn't see the duplication.** There were duplication-byte thresholds and `max_merge_bytes`. Most of the garbage is superseded versions of a relatively small set of large, frequently rewritten `TaskData` values, so those triggers missed it and produced inefficient merge groups.

### New Compaction policy
- **Shards:** each family's key space is split into power-of-two hash-prefix shards. The count starts at `FamilyConfig::initial_shard_bits` (TaskData 8 shards, TaskMeta 4, TaskCache and Infra 1) and then follows the family's size, targeting about 256 MB per shard.
  - It doubles once shards exceed 1.5× the target and halves below 0.5×, so a size near a boundary doesn't flip it.
  - Commits and merges split SST files at shard boundaries, so each shard is compacted on its own. Files written with an old count are re-split by their shard's next merge, not by a rewrite.
  - Write batches still buffer a family in at most 4 collectors (64 MB each) as on canary, split by a prefix of the shard bits, so their memory doesn't grow with the shard count. Families with more than 4 shards write proportionally smaller commit files.
- **Bottom merge:** when the files above a shard's bottom run exceed 50% of it, the whole shard is merged into a new bottom run. Tombstones count as the entries they delete. This is the merge that reliably drops superseded entries and tombstones.
    - This is analogous to a 'full compaction' but it targets a single shard and is targeting files covering typically <0.5G of data.
- **Intermediate merge:** more than 4 files above the bottom run are merged together, which bounds the number of files a lookup consults.
- **Budget:** bottom merges per family stop after rewriting 3× the family's fresh (not yet compacted) bytes, so cost follows new writes and shards spread over multiple compactions. 3× is how often a written byte is copied in steady state: a bottom merge at the 50% trigger rewrites 1.5× the bytes above the bottom run for every 0.5× of them.
- **Hard cap:** a shard over twice the trigger (100% space amplification), or with more than twice `max_files_above_bottom` files above its bottom run, is bottom-merged even when the budget is spent. This bounds how far a shard can fall behind, e.g. after a GC purge: its tombstones count as the entries they delete, but they're small and give little budget. 
- **Tiny families:** a 1 MB floor keeps families like Infra, which rewrite ~everything on every commit, out of bottom merges.
- **Ranking:** jobs are ranked across families by how far over their trigger they are, so intermediate merges aren't starved.

**Hot/cold split, only in bottom merges.** A bottom merge writes recently read keys and the rest into separate hot and cold files. It always includes every file of its shard, hot and cold, so this does not interfere with deduplication. Used-key tracking is unchanged from canary: each commit records the keys it read in its meta file, and compaction uses the union of all live meta files. The marks are never copied into meta files written by compaction, so they expire with the commit that recorded them.
    - This Hot/cold split is less aggressive than canary.  See below for Read locality impacts.

**Reads:** a lookup only consults the SST files of its key's shard. A per-family index keeps each shard's hash ranges densely, newest first, so lookups scan them sequentially.

## Verification

- The cache size benchmark above: vercel-site, 31 commits, GC with `rootTtlMs=0`. Earlier runs on the same base reproduce the GC-on results (canary 3.93–3.99 GB, this PR 3.00–3.05 GB).
- **Read locality**, measured with temporary instrumentation that isn't part of this PR. It counts the distinct SST blocks each build reads, and the distinct 128 KiB file regions they touch as an estimate of squashfs decompression. Same base, same builds, builds 2–31, GC on:

  | | canary | no split | this PR (bottom split) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | distinct blocks read per build, median | 1.35 GB | 1.80 GB | 1.55 GB |
  | 128 KiB regions touched per build, median / total | 2.42 / 64.2 GB | — | 2.63 / 68.8 GB |

  The bottom split recovers most of the locality that dropping the split cost. Light builds still read about a third more than on canary, because a shard's hot set only refreshes at its bottom merge. Splitting intermediate merges as well gained about 1%, so it isn't included.
- **Lookup microbenchmark**, 16 shards × 20 uncompacted commits (320 SSTs), alternating before and after: `get` hit −14%, miss −28%, `batch_get` −5%.
- `cargo test -p turbo-persistence` and `cargo test -p turbo-tasks-backend --tests` pass. The selector has unit tests, and a simulation whose sweep supports the 50% threshold.

pulls.title: fix(incremental-cache): keep an ISR entry's cache lifetime across instances and restarts
pulls.body:
### What?

An on-demand ISR page (dynamic route with `revalidate`, not prerendered at build) loses its `Cache-Control` header when the process serving it from the cache is not the one that rendered it. That happens with several instances sharing a cache handler, and with a single instance after a restart, including the default file-system cache.

After a restart it is also served `STALE` on every request, because `calculateRevalidate` falls back to its 1-second default.

A running instance can also retain an outdated lifetime after another instance replaces the shared entry with a shorter-lived result.

### Why?

`IncrementalCache.get()` takes an entry's lifetime only from `SharedCacheControls`: an in-memory map that `IncrementalCache.set()` fills in the same process, with the prerender manifest as fallback. An on-demand page of a dynamic route is not in the manifest. So any other process has no lifetime for the entry, sends no header, and treats the entry as stale after one second.

### How?

- `CacheHandlerValue` gets an optional `cacheControl`. Handlers already receive it as `ctx.cacheControl` in `set()`; now they can return it from `get()`.
- In `IncrementalCache.get()`, the lifetime returned with the entry takes precedence over the in-memory map and is remembered for the route, so both the response header and revalidation use the entry's current lifetime.
- The default `FileSystemCache` stores `cacheControl` in the `.meta` file of App Router pages and routes, and returns it.

Pages Router ISR is not covered: the file-system cache writes no `.meta` for it. I kept that out of this PR.

### Tests

`test/production/app-dir/isr-cache-control-restart` contains three separate on-disk fixture apps:

- `default`: the built-in file-system cache, with `cacheComponents: false`.
- `custom`: a persistent custom cache handler that stores `ctx.cacheControl`, with `cacheComponents: false`.
- `cache-components`: `cacheLife` with a persistent custom route-cache handler, covering the same on-demand route-cache path with Cache Components enabled.

The three restart cases render an on-demand page, age the entry beyond two seconds, and restart the server without rebuilding. The first response after restart must retain the original `Cache-Control` and report `HIT`; a repeat request must also report `HIT`. Aging past the broken one-second fallback makes the freshness assertion meaningful.

A fourth test keeps servers A and B running from the same build with one shared cache handler and a controllable service. A first caches a success with a one-hour lifetime. After direct eviction from the shared store, B caches an error result with a two-second lifetime. A must use the replacement entry's shorter `Cache-Control` and report `STALE` after two seconds. Direct eviction avoids relying on the fixture handler's no-op tag invalidation.

All four tests pass locally with Webpack and with Turbopack under `__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS=true`. The new two-server test catches the previous implementation retaining A's one-hour lifetime. The three restart cases were also verified to fail on the original PR base (`1cc0f661`) with `STALE` instead of `HIT`. Prettier, ESLint, the root and Next.js type checks, and the full repository build pass.

The local validation above ran on `7adcd57b`, before the subsequent merge of `canary` (`d093eb45`). That merge preserved the changed incremental-cache files and fixtures.

Fixes #99288

pulls.title: test: add PPF coverage to use-cache and RDC tests
pulls.body:
We weren't running the use-cache/resume-data-cache test suites in PPF. some of the tests fail due to the bug that is fixed in #98005 (although interestingly the fetch-cache tests only fail in deploy mode, because in `next start` we heal a bad RDC using outputs from `.next/cache/fetch-cache`). a bunch of refactoring was needed (some tests were producing false negatives, flakily), so i split this into a separate PR to confirm behavior before/after the fix.

### `use-cache.test.ts`

- I've refactored the tests to use timestamps and be a bit more debuggable. previously, they'd fail with a hydration error, and it was hard to pinpoint the cause. including a name lets us know which cache was mismatched, and assert that the values of the cache are consistent across the HTML shell / resume.
- the tests for exluded caches now include more complete assertions on what content is and isn't included in the HTML shell

### `resume-data-cache.test.ts`

This one needed quite a bit of work:

- The `use cache` and `fetch cache`  tests were not independent. they both used the same page and revalidated the same tag, which means that a revalidation from the first test affected the outcome of the second test. i've split them into two separate pages with two separate tags to make the behavior consistent.
- Multiple tests fetched the same URL (with `fetch(..., { cache: 'force-cache' }`), which made them interfere with each other's fetch caches. the URLs are now different so the tests are actually independent
- Some cache values are now tagged with a name and timestamp. The name is used for asserting consistency, the timestamp is for improved debuggability (provides ordering)
- The action revalidation tests weren't checking what the value from the build-time prerender was actually supposed to be, so they were passing even if the build-time RDC was not used at all
- The tests that use `browser()` now assert that there should be no hydration warning, which can happen due to the  PPF bug (due to inconsistent cache values across HTML shell/resume)
- **the revalidation assertions are very flaky in deploy**, and i've had to disable them to avoid introducing a test that fails often. i'm not sure how they were passing before.

pulls.title: Exclude metadata files from route handler type validation
pulls.body:
## Summary

Metadata files such as `app/icon.tsx` export a default handler, rather than HTTP methods. Validating them as ordinary route handlers rejects the documented `size` and `contentType` exports with TS2559 during `next typegen` + `tsc`.

Exclude metadata files from ordinary route-handler validation in both validator modes by matching the `route.<extension>` file convention, including custom page extensions. Add an icon fixture with the documented exports and a regression test that checks generated validation, retains an ordinary route-handler control, and runs `tsc`.

Correct the existing non-strict invalid-page-props assertion as well. The same failure reproduces on the unchanged base commit: non-strict `AppPageConfig` accepts arbitrary props, so the per-page check emits the invalid-props diagnostic instead. The test still requires a failed build and the specific invalid-props error; strict mode retains its `AppPageConfig` assertion.

## Verification

- Reproduced the stale assertion on unchanged base commit `3932a6bd516`: 12/13 tests passed, with only invalid-page-props failing.
- Full Webpack validator suite: **14/14 passed** in normal mode and **14/14 passed** with `__NEXT_EXPERIMENTAL_STRICT_ROUTE_TYPES=true`. Both runs include the icon regression and invalid ordinary-handler checks.
- Core Next.js build (including types), formatting, and ESLint passed.
- Direct before/after checks verified that both generators exclude metadata files while retaining ordinary and custom-extension route handlers.
- Tests use `NEXT_SKIP_ISOLATE=1` because the isolated install cannot resolve the configured package registry. Full bootstrap in the temporary worktree hit environment restrictions; the core package build passed.

pulls.title: fix: revalidateTag not reaching custom cache handlers when profiles differ
pulls.body:
Fix `updateTags` skipping cache handlers when a request uses multiple cache profiles.

## Why

`getCacheHandlers()` returns a one-time iterator. When tags are grouped by profile, the first group consumes the iterator, so subsequent groups don't reach any handlers.

This is especially noticeable with custom cache handlers, where tags may not be propagated to other instances.

## How

Convert the handlers iterator to an array once and reuse it for each profile group.

## Test

Added an E2E test covering `updateTag()` and `revalidateTag()` with different profiles.

Fixes #99352

pulls.title: Scope client component loading metrics to HTML renders
pulls.body:
## Summary

To measure how client component loading affects HTML render performance, replace telemetry based on process-global counters and incoming request-body completion. Those boundaries mixed overlapping renders and measured a lifecycle unrelated to HTML production.

Scope the counters and reporting context to each HTML-producing render. Start tracking before SSR, finish dynamic measurements at React readiness (Node `onAllReady` / Web `allReady`), and finish prerendering when the prerender operation returns. Preparation, action execution, and dedicated Flight rendering do not start tracking. DATA-only resumes finish tracking locally without waiting for output; an empty tracker emits no span. HTML rendered after a form action is still measured.

Already-started loads may settle and report afterward without keeping the response open. Preserve the first-write performance snapshot, but remove metrics stream wrapping and binding. This advances the larger effort to remove req/res lifecycle assumptions from App Router rendering without adding telemetry to `after()`.

Behavioral tests cover overlapping renders in both completion orders, HTML after a form POST, enhanced actions that only produce Flight, and HTML readiness while unused Flight content remains blocked.

## Verification

- Confirmed both new boundary regressions failed before the runtime change.
- Five behavioral metrics cases pass in development and production with both Turbopack and Webpack.
- Full production Turbopack instrumentation suite: 109 passed, 13 existing skips.
- Focused logger/response-piping units: 11 passed. Full repository build, package/root types, scoped Prettier, ESLint, and diff checks pass.
- A broader unit run passed 3,065 tests but hit three macOS `/var` versus `/private/var` assertions in unchanged TypeScript CLI tests.

Existing Node response-disconnect propagation to upstream SSR is unchanged; this PR does not claim to fix cancellation.

pulls.title: fix: preserve HTTP status codes during prerendering
pulls.body:
## Summary

Set the correct HTTP status and redirect location when a prerendered page throws `notFound()`, `unauthorized()`, `forbidden()`, `redirect()`, or `permanentRedirect()` inside Suspense. Preserve the prerendered layout and Suspense fallback so the client can recover at the appropriate error boundary.

Redirects take precedence over HTTP access fallbacks. Among access fallbacks, or among redirects, the first observed error wins. The HTML error callback and prerender recovery catch share this rule, so a later fatal not-found error cannot overwrite an already captured redirect. The catch still classifies its own error independently of the selected response.

Request-time streaming behavior is unchanged. A dynamic not-found after `connection()` can still return 200. The custom error UI itself is not prerendered and remains a follow-up.

Related: [NAR-435](https://linear.app/vercel/issue/NAR-435/set-status-code-on-prerendered-output-whenever-notfound-or-redirect).

## Verification

- All 57 production Turbopack tests pass with Cache Components enabled and disabled, with `__NEXT_EXPERIMENTAL_STRICT_ROUTE_TYPES=true`. This includes 44 ordered-error cases covering sibling Suspense boundaries and the outer recovery catch, status/location consistency, and preserved layout/fallback HTML.
- Removing the precedence fix causes 22 regression cases to fail.
- All 36 existing on-demand prerender recovery tests pass with Cache Components enabled: `NEXT_SKIP_ISOLATE=1 NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 __NEXT_EXPERIMENTAL_STRICT_ROUTE_TYPES=true __NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS=true pnpm test-start-turbo test/e2e/app-dir/on-demand-prerender-error-boundary/on-demand-prerender-error-boundary.test.ts`.
- Dev gate verified: all 57 tests are skipped.
- Local tests used the installed SWC canary.38 binary with Next.js canary.42 and emitted a version mismatch warning. Deploy mode was not run locally.

pulls.title: Turbopack: skip trimmed side-effect imports in SideEffectsModule
pulls.body:
A star re-export barrel with imports but no top-level side effects is
classified ModuleEvaluationIsSideEffectFree. follow_reexports_with_side_effects
treats that as effectful and builds a SideEffectsModule that emits
TURBOPACK_IMPORT(<eval part id>), but compute_side_effect_free_module_info
classifies the same module as side-effect-free, so binding-usage prunes the
Evaluation edge and the eval part never gets a module id. The build then
panicked with 'ModuleId not found for ident: .../barrel.ts <internal part 0>'
during middleware chunking.

SideEffectsModule is designed so graph tree-shaking may trim these imports, so
the consumer must tolerate a trimmed side effect. Add
ModuleIdStrategy::try_get_id_from_module (returns None instead of erroring when
an explicit id map lacks the module) and have chunk_item_content skip side
effects with no id -- a pruned side-effect-free module has nothing to evaluate.

Adds an e2e regression test (treeshake-mw).
